I have stopped reading a lot of novels. What actually happened in our own real world is fascinating enough, and avoids appeals to emotion that are often in novels (usually).

I have an illness and am not sure if it will be 4 years or 15 years, but I want to learn as much as I can about this crazy world while I can still smile in wonder - even if we forget it all at the last.

That is not to denigrate novels, they have a time and a place for everyone, Hemingway wrote novels that changed my perception of life. However not all novels click with all people and I end up wasting time. I kept trying to read Faulkner and could appreciate his artistry, other than that I came away with not much. James Joyce had a similar effect one me, obviously he was a master author of his time, but I quit Joyce after "Portrait of Artist.." and I "got" the journey towards self actualization, but found his imposition of experimental style to be distracting and sometimes it felt forced. The simple "Siddhartha" by Hermann Hesse was much more affecting for me in conveying and allowing the reader to taste the flavor of the journey towards knowing your true self.

Many would disagree with me on all of the above. Good Non-fiction is generally universal when not tinged by "presentism" and/or a judgmental author really writing about their own value system and using history to share it with the reader.

So I waste less time with admired non-fiction than novels overall.

To answer your question I have read Gaijin, Tai-pan, and other Clavell novels. He writes great period fiction that is very entertaining.

I am sticking to non-fiction now unless people who know me a bit overwhelmingly recommend a certain novel, then I will read it.

Thank you both for your suggestions, can anyone else suggest something on this period in Japanese history that they have read and admire?

The Making of Modern Japan by Marius B. Jansen has been one of the best texts for modern Japanese history, but it obviously covers more than just the Meiji Restoration. Still, if you need a broad overview first, it would work.

For more concentrated works, I'd recommend checking out Sakamoto Ryoma and the Meiji Restoration, also by Marius B. Jansen, and The Autobiography of Yukichi Fukuzawa. I love to study the Meiji period as well, but more on the literature side of things (because their literature also underwent extraordinarily rapid changes).

Also, it seems W. G. Beasley has a book called The Meiji Restoration that looks highly rated and lauded as the best on the subject. I'll have to check it out too! Though it was published over 40 years ago, if you're concerned about that sort of thing.
I second Jansen. He was on our reading list in my college course on JPN history Pre-WW2.

I'm reading a great book right now called The Great Wave: Gilded Age Misfits, Japanese Eccentrics and the Opening of Old Japan by Christopher Benfey. It basically tells the story of a couple key players in the early years of the opening/modernization of Japan. It's not a cut and dry academic overview of what exactly went into modernization or how it was done, but it does largely touch on it by talking about the lives of the people who played key roles.

Great subject by the way. I'd love to hear recommendations as well.

Guayana Esequiba (Spanish pronunciation: [ɡwaˈʝana eseˈkiβa]) is a territory administered by Guyana but claimed by Venezuela. It was first included in the Viceroyalty of New Granada and the Captaincy General of Venezuela by Spain, but was later included in Essequibo by the Dutch and in British Guiana by the United Kingdom. Originally, parts of what is now eastern Venezuela were included in the disputed area. The portion today under the administration of Guyana divides the area in six administrative regions (Barima-Waini, Cuyuni-Mazaruni, Pomeroon-Supenaam, Potaro-Siparuni, Upper Takutu-Upper Essequibo and Essequibo Islands-West Demerara), while Venezuela treats it as a single entity (Guayana Esequiba or "Zona en Reclamación"). This territory of 159,500 km² is the subject of a long-running boundary dispute inherited from the colonial powers and complicated by the independence of Guyana in 1966. The status of the territory is subject to the Treaty of Geneva, which was signed by the United Kingdom, Venezuela and British Guiana governments on February 17, 1966. This treaty stipulates that the parties will agree to find a practical, peaceful and satisfactory solution to the dispute. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guayana_Esequiba
